First listed 2025-12-05 · episode or wrap

The Housing Market is Broken: Why Homes Are Unaffordable & What It Takes to Fix It | The Weekly Wrap

Eisman argues that mortgage lock-in, constrained local supply and rising ownership costs explain housing’s weakness despite better-run builders. He distinguishes builders from companies exposed to existing-home transactions and favors supply reforms over buyer subsidies. FHFA loan-level research supports the lock-in mechanism; other quantitative and causal claims need matched evidence. He also discusses AI risks to software franchises, skepticism about crypto valuation and ETF structure. His practical fund comparison is mostly sound, but passive portfolios do change with their indices and not every mutual fund is actively managed.

  • Updated investor bulletin on exchange-traded funds · 2023-02-23
    Retail ETF shares trade in secondary markets. Authorized participants create/redeem large units, typically with in-kind baskets. ETF selling therefore need not mechanically cause an equivalent cash sale by the fund; index and ETF flow effects require separate analysis.

How he reasons here

  • Separate new-home and existing-home transaction exposure.
  • Compare earnings deterioration with stock expectations before assuming fundamentals are improving.
  • Model mortgage payments explicitly and distinguish liquidity lock-in from construction constraints.
  • Compare demand subsidies with supply elasticity.
  • Evaluate fund structure, costs and taxes separately from manager skill.

Tools and charts discussed

Mentioned in the transcript; visual charts have not all been inspected.

  • Builder and building-product company EPS and share-return tables
  • Zelman entry-level affordability index including taxes and insurance
  • Illustrative $400,000 thirty-year mortgage at 4% and 6.25%
  • Mortgage rate distribution, public builder market share and housing shortage estimates
  • ETF fees, trading, disclosure and in-kind redemption
